newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland shifts powers from president to parliament.
newsitem.headline: Poland shifts powers from president to parliament.

text.p: The new constitution being put to a referendum on Sunday strips Poland's presidency of important powers and shifts the balance in parliament's favour.
Opinion is sharply divided over whether this would be good for Poland's eight-year-old democracy or not.
Current President Aleksander Kwasniewski, whose fellow ex-communists now dominate parliament and could win a new term in elections this year, is content to lose some major powers.

But former incumbent Lech Walesa, who as the first directly-elected president after the fall of communism fought to uphold the authority of his office, sees it as a disaster and called on compatriots to reject the new constitution.
"I have always said that in this period of Poland's transformation we need a presidential system, with decrees," Walesa told Reuters in his home city Gdansk.
He argued that such decrees, subject to later parliamentary approval, would allow decisive action where required.
The new constitution, which would replace the 1952 Stalin-era charter amended in 1992 by a makeshift interim "small" constitution, moves in the opposite direction.
The president will no longer be able to use his veto to block the national budget -- a weapon Walesa brandished in 1994 against his ex-communist foes and their allies in government.
A smaller parliamentary majority, three-fifths rather than two-thirds, will suffice to overrule his veto on other issues.

The new constitution ends the president's ability to nominate the foreign, interior and defence ministers -- by which Walesa foisted his candidates on a reluctant cabinet, thus ensuring a non-party or opposition presence in key posts.
No longer will the president, who is directly elected every five years, be able to appoint a temporary cabinet if a deadlocked parliament cannot agree on one.

These changes were developed by the ex-communists, drafting the constitution at a time when they were desperate to get Walesa off their backs and had no guarantee their own candidate would beat him in the 1995 elections.
Kwasniewski says they merely fine-tune the balance.

"From the start, Poland's presidency has been half way between a system of a strong presidency like France, and systems with much weaker presidents like in Hungary, the Czech republic or Germany," he told Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper.
"I share the view that Poland is not now ready for either a parliamentary-cabinet or a presidential system. We still need many, many years of experience," he said in a pre-referendum radio interview.
Kwasniewski may yet feel the effects of his diminished authority if, like Walesa, he is confronted after the elections by a parliament dominated by hostile rightist parties.
For Lech Falandysz, the lawyer who helped Walesa squeeze every drop of influence from the presidency and who favours a French model, the proposed new arrangements are pointless.

"The people will be uselessly bothered voting in direct national elections for a president, under the illusion they are choosing a real executive...when in fact they are picking a kind of king who can say nice things on television but cannot resolve anything else," he told Reuters.
For much of history Poland has been wrestling to find the right relationship between executive and legislature.
In the 18th century a chaotic parliamentary system for nobles with absurd rights of veto, dominating an elected monarchy, weakened Poland so badly it was dismembered by neighbours.

When it gained independence after World War One, it decided on weak presidential powers, underwent a coup by strongman Jozef Pilsudski, and finally adopted a strong presidency a few years before being engulfed by German and Soviet invasion in World War Two.
